newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: NEW S.AFRICAN LABOUR DISPUTE BODY KEPT BUSY.
newsitem.headline: NEW S.AFRICAN LABOUR DISPUTE BODY KEPT BUSY.

text.p: More than 19,000 cases were referred to the Commission for Conciliation, Mediation and Arbitration (CCMA) during its first six months in operation, of which about 50 percent had been settled, co-ordinator Charles Nupen said on Monday.
"Fifty percent is not bad...but we could be doing better," he told a parliamentary committee.

The CCMA was set up in terms of the new Labour Relations Act to provide quick and fair mediation in labour disputes, especially those involving small employers and unorganised workers, including domestic and farm workers.

Because of the high workload, Nupen said it had become clear that more staff would have to be recruited to deal with cases. The CCMA planned to take on 40 more full-time commissioners over the next few months as well as about 40 part-time commissioners.
Nupen said that 37 percent of the cases had come from Gauteng, 20 percent from KwaZulu-Natal, 14 percent from the Western Cape and the balance from the other six provinces.

Nineteen percent of the cases involved workers in commercial distribution. The other main sectors involved included the food and beverage sector, private security firms, building and construction and domestic and farm workers.
He admitted that commission staff had been on a steep learning curve and had perhaps not paid as much attention as they should to dispute prevention rather than just dispute settlement.
Future legislation on issues such as employment equity could lead to more cases being referred to the commission.
Nupen said he hoped that the CCMA would be involved in the drafting of such legislation.
